subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If y = tan⁻¹√((1 − x)/(1 + x)), |x| < 1, find dy/dx.

mark_split.label: Simplify the square root to tan θ
Reduce y to half of cos⁻¹x

The mathematics was checked independently before writing: the reduction y = ½cos⁻¹x was confirmed numerically at x = 0.5, x = −0.3 and x = 0.9, and −1/(2√(1 − x²)) matched a central difference quotient at all three (−0.57735027, −0.52414242, −1.14707867). The |x| < 1 restriction printed in the stem is genuine and is used in the card: at x = −1 the fraction under the square root is undefined, and at x = ±1 the derivative of cos⁻¹x does not exist.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what you substitute for x, and what the square root becomes after that.

steps.label: Substitute x = cos 2θ
steps.margin_note: First mark. Choosing cos 2θ rather than sin θ or tan θ is the whole decision here. It is chosen because 1 − cos 2θ and 1 + cos 2θ are both perfect squares, which is what removes the square root.
lines: Let y = tan⁻¹√((1 − x)/(1 + x)),  where |x| < 1
Put x = cos 2θ,  so that 2θ = cos⁻¹x  and  θ = ½cos⁻¹x
Since |x| < 1, cos⁻¹x lies in (0, π), so 2θ lies in (0, π) and θ lies in (0, π/2)

recall.must_convey: That x is replaced by cos 2θ, so that θ = ½cos⁻¹x.

steps.why: Differentiating the expression as it stands needs the chain rule three times, on the inverse tangent, the square root and the quotient. The substitution replaces all of that with two half-angle identities and one differentiation.
common_mistakes: Substituting x = cos θ instead of cos 2θ, which leaves half-angles and does not simplify.
Differentiating directly with three nested chain rules, which is correct but long and easily lost.
steps.memory_tip: When 1 − x and 1 + x both appear, put x = cos 2θ. The two half-angle identities then turn the pair into 2sin²θ and 2cos²θ.

steps.label: Simplify the square root to tan θ
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Quote both half-angle identities. Say why the square root is +tan θ and not ±tan θ: θ lies in (0, π/2), so tan θ is positive there.
lines: θ lies in (0, π/2), so tan θ > 0

recall.must_convey: That the half-angle identities turn the fraction into tan²θ, so the square root is tan θ.

steps.why: √(tan²θ) is |tan θ|, not tan θ, in general. The range of θ fixed in step 1 is what allows the modulus to be dropped, so the two parts of the working depend on each other.
common_mistakes: Writing √(tan²θ) as tan θ without checking the sign, which is only true because θ is in (0, π/2).
Mixing the identities up and using 1 − cos 2θ = 2cos²θ.
steps.memory_tip: Remember the pair by which function survives: 1 MINUS cos 2θ keeps the SINE, 1 PLUS cos 2θ keeps the COSINE.

steps.why: The whole point of the substitution is that a complicated inverse tangent becomes a simple inverse cosine. Once y = ½cos⁻¹x is written, the question is a one-line differentiation.
common_mistakes: Writing y = θ without checking that θ lies in the principal range of tan⁻¹.
Forgetting the factor ½ and writing y = cos⁻¹x.
steps.memory_tip: The 2 in cos 2θ becomes the ½ in the answer. Track it from the substitution to the last line.

steps.label: Differentiate
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The minus sign belongs to cos⁻¹x and must survive to the final line. The answer is negative for every |x| < 1, which agrees with y decreasing as x increases.

steps.why: The restriction |x| < 1 printed in the question is what makes this line valid: at x = ±1 the denominator is zero and the derivative does not exist, and at x = −1 the original fraction is undefined as well.
common_mistakes: Dropping the minus sign by using the derivative of sin⁻¹x instead of cos⁻¹x.
Writing the 2 inside the square root as √(2(1 − x²)).
steps.memory_tip: sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ have the same derivative apart from the sign. This answer came from cos⁻¹, so it is the negative one.

insider_note: Put x = cos 2θ so the half-angle forms turn the fraction into tan²θ. Then y = θ = ½Cos⁻¹x, and the answer is half the Cos⁻¹ derivative.
